title: The birth of the United Nations
body: The UN Charter was signed in San Francisco on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October 1945, now celebrated as United Nations Day. The UN replaced the League of Nations, created after World War I.

title: The UN Security Council
body: The Security Council has 15 members. Five are permanent and hold a veto: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States. The other ten are elected for two-year terms.

title: 193 member states
body: As of 2025, the United Nations has 193 member states. South Sudan, in 2011, was the most recent country to join. Two observer states, the Holy See and Palestine, are not full members.
source_name: Wikipedia: Member states of the United Nations

title: The African Union
body: The African Union (AU) was launched in 2002 in Durban, South Africa, replacing the Organisation of African Unity. It has 55 member states and its headquarters are in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

title: Africa Day
body: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was founded on 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 independent African states. 25 May is celebrated as Africa Day.

title: SADC
body: The Southern African Development Community (SADC) promotes economic integration, peace and security in southern Africa. It was established in 1992, succeeding a coordination conference formed in 1980. Its headquarters are in Gaborone, Botswana.

title: ECOWAS
body: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was founded by the Treaty of Lagos on 28 May 1975 to promote economic integration in West Africa. Its headquarters are in Abuja, Nigeria.

title: The European Union
body: The European Union is a political and economic union of European countries. As of 2025 it has 27 member states, after the United Kingdom left in 2020. Most members use the euro as their currency.

title: NATO
body: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is a military alliance founded in 1949. Under Article 5 of its treaty, an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

title: Embassies and consulates
body: An embassy is a country's main diplomatic mission in a foreign capital, led by an ambassador. Consulates are smaller offices, often in other cities, that help citizens abroad and issue visas.

title: Diplomatic immunity
body: The 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations sets the rules for diplomacy, including diplomatic immunity: diplomats cannot be prosecuted by the host country, though they can be expelled.
source_name: Wikipedia: Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations

title: The Peace of Westphalia
body: The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War in Europe. It is often seen as the origin of the modern idea of sovereign states that do not interfere in each other's internal affairs.

title: Bretton Woods, 1944
body: At the Bretton Woods conference in New Hampshire, USA, in July 1944, 44 Allied nations agreed a new international monetary system and created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.

title: The World Trade Organization
body: The World Trade Organization (WTO) began on 1 January 1995, replacing the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947. It sets rules for trade between nations and settles trade disputes. It is based in Geneva.

title: BRICS
body: BRICS began as a grouping of Brazil, Russia, India and China; South Africa joined in 2010. The group expanded from 2024 with new members including Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates.

title: The Non-Aligned Movement
body: The Non-Aligned Movement was founded in Belgrade in 1961 by countries that chose not to formally join either side in the Cold War. Leaders of India, Egypt, Yugoslavia, Ghana and Indonesia played key roles.

title: Hard power and soft power
body: Hard power is getting what you want through force or payment, like military action or sanctions. Soft power, a term coined by Joseph Nye, is attraction: culture, values and policies that make others want to cooperate.

title: The Commonwealth
body: The Commonwealth of Nations is a voluntary association of 56 member countries, as of 2025, most of them former British territories. Gabon and Togo, which have no historic ties to Britain, joined in 2022.

title: The International Court of Justice
body: The International Court of Justice (ICJ), in The Hague, Netherlands, is the UN's main court. It settles legal disputes between states and gives advisory opinions. It has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms.

title: The International Criminal Court
body: The International Criminal Court (ICC), which began work in 2002 in The Hague, tries individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression. Unlike the ICJ, it prosecutes people, not states.

title: Economic sanctions
body: Sanctions are penalties one or more countries place on another, such as trade bans, frozen assets or travel bans, to pressure a change in behaviour without using military force.

title: The Geneva Conventions
body: The four Geneva Conventions of 1949 set rules for the humane treatment of wounded soldiers, prisoners of war and civilians during armed conflict. Every UN member state has ratified them.

title: The Paris Agreement
body: Adopted in December 2015, the Paris Agreement on climate change aims to keep global warming well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C.

title: The UN General Assembly
body: The General Assembly is the UN body where all 193 member states meet, each with one vote regardless of size. Its resolutions are mostly recommendations; binding decisions on peace and security come from the Security Council.

title: Bilateral and multilateral
body: Bilateral relations are between two countries, such as a trade deal between Kenya and India. Multilateral relations involve three or more countries, often through organisations such as the UN, the AU or the WTO.

title: Word: ratify
body: Meaning: to formally approve a treaty so it becomes legally binding on a country, usually through parliament.
example_sentence: Parliament voted to ratify the trade agreement.

title: Word: embargo
body: Meaning: an official ban on trade or other activity with a particular country.
example_sentence: The arms embargo banned all weapons sales to the region.

title: Word: envoy
body: Meaning: a messenger or representative sent by a government on a special diplomatic mission.
example_sentence: The UN sent a special envoy to help with peace talks.

title: Word: détente
body: Meaning: the easing of tension between rival countries. Often used for the Cold War period of the 1970s.
example_sentence: The summit marked a new détente between the two neighbours.

title: Word: bloc
body: Meaning: a group of countries that act together because of shared interests.
example_sentence: The trade bloc negotiated as one with larger economies.

title: Veto powers
body: UN check.
statement: The UN Security Council has five permanent members with a veto
explanation: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US can each veto Security Council resolutions.

title: AU headquarters
body: Africa check.
statement: The African Union's headquarters is in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia
explanation: The AU, like the OAU before it, is based in Addis Ababa.

title: SADC headquarters
body: Africa check.
statement: SADC's headquarters is in Nairobi, Kenya
explanation: SADC is based in Gaborone. Kenya is not a SADC member; it belongs to the East African Community.

title: When the UN began
body: History check.
statement: The United Nations was founded in 1919
explanation: The UN was founded in 1945 after World War II. The League of Nations came first, after World War I.

title: NATO's founding
body: History check.
explanation: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington in April 1949.

title: The World Court
body: International law check.
statement: The International Court of Justice is in The Hague
explanation: The ICJ sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague.

title: Why 25 May?
body: Africa check.
statement: Africa Day on 25 May marks the founding of the OAU in 1963
explanation: The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963.

title: From GATT to WTO
body: Trade check.
explanation: The WTO started on 1 January 1995 and took over the GATT rules.

title: Votes in the General Assembly
body: UN check.
statement: Every UN member state has one vote in the General Assembly
explanation: Each of the 193 members has one vote, whatever its size or wealth.

title: Bretton Woods
body: History check.
statement: The IMF and World Bank were created at the Bretton Woods conference in 1944
explanation: 44 Allied nations met at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944 and created both institutions.

title: The security dilemma
body: When one state arms to feel safe, its neighbours feel less safe and arm too. Both end up spending more and feeling less secure, even if neither wanted conflict. It is a central idea in realist theory.

title: Democratic peace theory
body: Established democracies have very rarely, if ever, fought wars against each other. Suggested reasons include accountable leaders, shared norms and trade ties, though scholars still debate the causes and the definitions.

title: The Thucydides trap
body: Political scientist Graham Allison argues that when a rising power threatens to displace a ruling one, war becomes more likely, as with Athens and Sparta. The idea is often applied to US–China rivalry, and is also widely criticised.

title: The Responsibility to Protect
body: Endorsed by all UN members in 2005, R2P says states must protect their people from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, and others may act if they fail. The 2011 Libya intervention made it controversial.
